The Goldspotted grenadier anchovy Coilia dussumieri attains a maximum recorded length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], a value characteristic of a small, fast-growing engraulid that occupies coastal and estuarine waters of the Indo-Pacific. Individuals reach the size at which they become reproductively active at 14.7 centimeters [Lp = 14.7 centimeters] total length, indicating that a substantial portion of somatic growth occurs prior to the onset of spawning activity. Field surveys in the Gulf of Thailand have consistently documented that sexually mature adults dominate the catches once they exceed this length threshold, suggesting that the transition to adulthood is closely tied to body size rather than chronological age alone. The species' maximum body mass, recorded from the largest senescent individuals in museum collections, is 29.3 grams [Wwi = 29.3 grams], reflecting a slender, laterally compressed body plan that is typical of anchovies exploiting plankton-rich, turbid environments. This ultimate wet weight is achieved only after several years of sustained somatic investment.

At the time of first spawning, females typically weigh 11.6 grams [Wwp = 11.6 grams], a mass that corresponds closely to the length-based estimate derived from the species' length-weight relationship. The onset of reproductive activity is therefore tightly coupled to a specific body mass threshold, rather than a purely temporal schedule. In terms of egg output, individuals spawn multiple times across a single breeding season. Gravid females produce approximately 58 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 58 eggs per clutch], and the interval between successive spawning events is relatively short, yielding 1 clutch per day [F_R_i = 1 clutch per day] when water temperatures are maintained at 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. Under these conditions, the daily reproduction rate reaches approximately 58 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 58 eggs per day]. This elevated daily fecundity represents a classic r-selected reproductive strategy, maximizing offspring production during the brief, productive monsoon-driven plankton blooms typical of the species' tropical habitat.

Hatching follows a short incubation period of only 9 days [ab = 9 days] at the ambient temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], a rapid developmental pace consistent with the warm, shallow nursery grounds where this anchovy deposits its adhesive, demersal eggs. The newly emerged prolarvae are minute; each individual carries a wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves contained within the 0.8 millimeter diameter egg. The egg diameter itself constrains the initial larval size at eclosion, and the low birth mass imposes an immediate need for efficient exogenous feeding once the yolk sac is resorbed. Prolonged incubation at cooler temperatures would delay hatching, but this species appears to be adapted to the consistently warm thermal regime of its equatorial environment. The yolk-sac stage is brief, with larvae progressing rapidly to first feeding within hours of chorion rupture.

Longevity records for Coilia dussumieri indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under natural conditions at 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], a relatively short duration that aligns with the species' high reproductive output and early maturation. The oldest individuals collected during mark-recapture studies in the Mekong Delta were aged at 48 months, confirming this upper bound. Because the species is semelparous only at the population level, with iteroparous adults spawning repeatedly within a season, the lifespan of 4 years allows for multiple reproductive bouts across two to three breeding seasons before senescence sets in. The physiological deterioration that culminates in natural mortality is likely linked to the depletion of lipid reserves following intensive spawning activity, a pattern observed in many small tropical clupeiforms.

When comparing the life-history traits of Coilia dussumieri with those of its congener Coilia nasus, the former exhibits a smaller maximum total length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters] and a lighter adult body mass of 29.3 grams [Wwi = 29.3 grams], indicative of a more abbreviated growth trajectory. Conversely, the puberty length of 14.7 centimeters [Lp = 14.7 centimeters] corresponds to a mass of 11.6 grams [Wwp = 11.6 grams], a point at which approximately 40 percent of the ultimate length has already been attained. This precocious sexual maturation relative to ultimate size is a hallmark of species inhabiting unpredictable environments where early reproduction carries a selective advantage. The species' high fecundity, combined with a 9-day egg development period (9 days) [ab = 9 days] at 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C] and a 4-year lifespan (4 years) [am = 4 years] at 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], classifies it firmly within a fast-lived, high-turnover life-history syndrome typical of small pelagic forage fish.
